{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In mathematics, the '''transfinite recursion theorem''' says a function can be defined using a recursion over a well-ordered set; for example, <math>\mathbb{N}</math> but also over general well-ordered sets.

Since each well-ordered set is isomorphic to an ordinal, the theorem is also often stated in terms of ordinals.

== Statements ==
Transfinite recursion is an instance of [[transfinite induction]] and the latter works over a well-ordered set (in fact, the feasibility of such an induction is equivalent to well-ordered-ness). In particular, the theorem can be stated for well-ordered sets. If <math>A</math> is a partially ordered set, we write <math>A^a = \{ b \in A \mid b < a \}.</math>

{{math_theorem|name=Transfinite recursion theorem <ref name=Halmos_18>{{harvnb|Halmos|1960|loc=§ 18.}}</ref>|math_statement=Let a set <math>X</math>, a well-ordered set <math>A</math> and a function
:<math>G : \{ A^a \to X \mid a \in A \} \to X</math>
be given. Then there exists a unique function
:<math>f : A \to X</math>
such that
:<math>f(a) = G(f|_{A^a})</math>
for each <math>a</math> in <math>A</math>, where the vertical bar means restriction.}}

The transfinite recursion theorem is also commonly stated for ordinals. One simple version is: let a set <math>X</math> and a class function <math>G</math> with values in <math>X</math> defined on the class of all functions be given. Then, for each ordinal <math>\alpha</math>, there exists a unique function
:<math>f : \alpha \to X</math>
such that, for every ordinal <math>\beta < \alpha</math>; that is, <math>\beta \in \alpha</math> or <math>\beta \subsetneq \alpha</math>,
:<math>f(\beta) = G(f|_{\beta})</math>.
Since an ordinal is a well-ordered set, the above version follows from the well-ordered version (as <math>\beta = \alpha^{\beta}</math>). Although it is common to ask <math>G</math> to be defined for all functions, this is just a convenient way of stating the theorem. In practice, one usually only defines <math>G(f)</math> for functions <math>f : \alpha \to X</math>, <math>\alpha</math> all ordinals, and then extends <math>G</math> for all other functions arbitrary.

== Proof ==
When <math>A = \mathbb{N}</math>, the proof here appears in N. Jacobson's ''Basic Algebra I''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Jacobson |first1=Nathan |title=Basic Algebra I: Second Edition |date=22 June 2009 |publisher=Courier Corporation |isbn=978-0-486-47189-1 |url=https://books.google.co.jp/books/about/Basic_Algebra_I.html?id=qAg_AwAAQBAJ&redir_esc=y |language=en |location=§ 0.4.}}</ref> and exactly the same proof goes through for an arbitrary well-ordered set. The proof itself is taken from Halmos.<ref name=Halmos_18 />

We say a subset <math>E \subset A \times X</math> is ''closed (with respect to <math>G</math>)'' if for each function <math>f : A^a \to X, \, a \in A</math> whose graph is contained in <math>E</math>, we have <math>(a, G(f))</math> is in <math>E</math>. For example, <math>A \times X</math> is closed.

Let <math>F</math> be the intersection of all closed subsets of <math>A \times X</math> (with respect to <math>G</math>), which is again closed. We shall prove <math>F</math> is a graph of a function <math>A \to X</math>; that is, the fiber <math>p^{-1}(a)</math> for the projection <math>p : F \subset A \times X \to A</math> has exactly one element for each <math>a</math> in <math>A</math>. For this, we shall use strong induction over <math>A</math>. That is, assuming <math>\# p^{-1}(b) = 1</math> for every <math>b < a</math>, we show <math>\# p^{-1}(a) = 1</math>.

By inductive hypothesis, we have the function <math>f : A^a \to X, \, b \mapsto \text{unique element in }p^{-1}(b)</math>. Note the graph of it lies in <math>F</math>. Since <math>F</math> is closed, <math>(a, G(f))</math> is in <math>F</math>. Thus, <math>\# p^{-1}(a) \ge 1</math>. To show it is the equality, suppose otherwise. That means there is some pair <math>(a, y) \ne (a, G(f))</math> in <math>F</math>. We claim the set
:<math>E := F - \{ (a, y) \}</math>
is closed. Thus, let <math>g : A^b \to X</math> be a function whose graph lies in <math>E</math>. If <math>b = a</math>, then we have <math>f = g</math> by inductive hypothesis; indeed, since their graphs lie in <math>F</math>,
:<math>\{ f(c), g(c) \} \subset p^{-1}(c)</math>
for each <math>c < a</math>. Thus, <math>(b, G(g)) \in E</math> since <math>y \neq G(f) = G(g)</math> and <math>F</math> is closed. If <math>b \ne a</math>, then again <math>(b, G(g))</math> is in <math>E</math> as <math>F</math> is closed. This proves the claim and then <math>E \subsetneq F</math> is a contradiction to the smallest-ness of <math>F</math>. Finally, the uniqueness holds by a similar but easier induction. <math>\square</math>

== Examples ==
=== Example: a basis construction ===
Let <math>V</math> be a vector space. There is a "very obvious" way to construct a basis of <math>V</math> as follows. If <math>V \ne 0</math>, pick a nonzero vector <math>v_1</math> and then pick another nonzero vector <math>v_2</math> not in the span of <math>v_1</math>, if any, and so on. Transfinite recursion can make this argument rigorous, as we now show (alternatively, one can use Zorn's lemma; see {{section link| Zorn's lemma|Every vector space has a basis}}.)

Let the above <math>V</math> be given a well-ordering by the [[well-ordering theorem]]. Suppose we are given a sequence of vectors <math>x_{\gamma}</math> indexed by an ordinal <math>\beta</math>. That is, we are given a function <math>f : \beta \to V</math> such that <math>f(\gamma) = x_{\gamma}</math> for each <math>\gamma \in \beta</math> (or <math>\gamma < \beta</math>). Then let
:<math>G(f) =</math> the least element in the complement <math>V - \operatorname{span}(\operatorname{im}(f))</math>
if <math>V \ne \operatorname{span}(\operatorname{im}(f))</math> and <math>G(f) = 0</math> otherwise. Note, since <math>f</math> is arbitrary, the image of <math>f</math> is not necessarily linearly independent; all we have is that <math>G(f)</math> is linearly independent from the nonzero vectors in <math>\operatorname{im}(f)</math>.

The transfinite recursion theorem then says: given an ordinal <math>\alpha</math>, there exists a unique <math>f : \alpha \to V</math> that satisfies the recursion condition; i.e., <math>f(\beta) = G(f|_{\beta})</math> is linearly independent from <math>\operatorname{im}(f|_{\beta})</math> for <math>\beta < \alpha</math>. In particular, the nonzero vectors in the image of <math>f</math> are linearly independent. Finally, if we take <math>\alpha = \kappa</math> to be some large ordinal; e.g., take <math>\kappa</math> to have cardinality strictly larger than that of <math>V</math>, then, for the reason of cardinality,
:<math>B := \operatorname{im}(f : \kappa \to V) - \{ 0 \}</math>
is a basis of <math>V</math>. (Note, unlike a construction by Zorn's lemma, this basis is uniquely determined by a choice of a well-ordering on <math>V</math>.)

=== Example: a proof of Zorn's lemma ===
Transfinite recursion is used in a typical proof of [[Zorn's lemma]], assuming the axiom of choice. Here is an argument (which is fairly similar to the construction of a basis above).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~kbrown/6310/zorn.pdf|format=PDF|title=Mathematics 6310 : Zorn's lemma|author=Ken Brown|location=[[Cornell University]]|date=September 2010|website=Pi.math.cornell.edu|access-date=June 20, 2026}}</ref>

Let <math>X</math> be a partially ordered set in which each chain, including the empty chain, has an upper bound. To show <math>X</math> has a maximal element, suppose, on the contrary, that it has none. Then each chain <math>C</math> has a strict upper bound; i.e., an element <math>x</math> in <math>X</math> such that <math>x > y</math> for each <math>y</math> in <math>C</math>, since it has an upper bound which is bounded by some strictly larger element. Let <math>c : \mathfrak{P}(X) - \{ \emptyset \} \to X</math> be a choice function; i.e., <math>c(S) \in S</math> and then for each chain <math>C</math> in <math>X</math>, let
:<math>b(C) = c(\{ \text{strict upper bounds of }C \}).</math>
We now recursively construct a sequence over ordinals. For each function <math>f : \beta \to X</math>, let <math>G(f) = b(\operatorname{im}(f))</math> if <math>\operatorname{im}(f)</math> is a chain and otherwise <math>G(f) = </math> some arbitrary element in <math>X</math>; e.g., <math>b(\emptyset)</math>. By the transfinite recursion theorem, we find a function <math>f : \alpha \to X</math> such that <math>f(\beta) = G(f|_{\beta})</math> for <math>\beta < \alpha</math>; in particular, it is injective. But this is a contradiction since there is an ordinal whose cardinality is strictly larger than that of <math>X</math> (see [[Hartogs number]]). If one is not sure about the existence of a large ordinal, there is also an argument that avoids ordinals altogether (still using transfinite recursion). See e.g., {{section link|Hausdorff maximal principle#Proof from the well-ordering theorem}}.
<math>\square</math>

== Recursion with the axiom of replacement ==
{{see also|Well-founded relation#Induction and recursion}}
For some use of transfinite recursion, we may need to construction a function with values in a class; in that case, we need to use the [[axiom of replacement]] to ensure we still get the function <math>f</math> even though the codomain is a class.

Here is an example of such a need.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2009/01/28/245b-notes-7-well-ordered-sets-ordinals-and-zorns-lemma-optional/|title=Theorem 1 in 245B, Notes 7: Well-ordered sets, ordinals, and Zorn's lemma (optional)|website=Terrytao.wordpress.com|access-date=June 20, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Halmos|1960|loc=§ 20., Counting theorem.}}</ref> Suppose we want to show
:Each well-ordered set is uniquely isomorphic to a unique ordinal.
The problem is that, ''a priori'', we don’t know what ordinal to use. Thus, at each stage in transfinite induction, we construct a new ordinal. Precisely, given a well-ordered set <math>X</math> and an element <math>a</math> in <math>X</math>, suppose we have constructed
:<math>g_b : X^b \overset{\sim}\to \alpha_b</math>
where <math>X^b = \{ c \mid c < b \}</math>. We shall extend these isomorphisms to an isomorphism <math>X^a \simeq \alpha</math> for some ordinal <math>\alpha</math>. If <math>a = s(b)</math> is a successor; i.e., the least element among strict upper bounds of <math>b</math>, then we let <math>f|_{X^b} = g_b</math> and <math>f(a) = \alpha_b</math>. Then
:<math>f : X^a \overset{\sim}\to s(\alpha_b) := \alpha_b \cup \{ \alpha_b \},</math>
where the union on the right exists by the [[axiom of union]]. If <math>a = \sup(X^a)</math>, then, thinking <math>g_b</math> as sets of ordered pairs, let
:<math>f = \bigcup_{b < a} g_b.</math>
The union on the right is a ''set'' by the axiom of replacement and the axiom of union; indeed, the former guarantees the collection <math>\{ g_b \mid b < a \}</math> is a set. Let <math>\alpha</math> be the image of <math>f</math>, which is clearly an ordinal, and <math>f : X^a \overset{\sim}\to \alpha</math>. Finally, we check the uniqueness. By transfinite induction, we see isomorphisms between ordinals are the identities. Then given <math>f : X \overset{\sim}\to \alpha, g : X \overset{\sim}\to \beta</math>, we have <math>g \circ f^{-1} : \alpha \overset{\sim}\to \beta</math> is the identity and so <math>f = g</math>. <math>\square</math>

The same argument can be used to prove the transfinite recursion theorem when the target <math>X</math> is a class. The proof is by strong induction over ordinals (the same proof works for well-ordered sets but we use ordinals for simplicity). Thus, assume the theorem is true for every <math>\beta < \alpha</math>. By inductive hypothesis, for each <math>\beta < \alpha</math>, we have a unique function <math>g_{\beta} : \beta \to X</math> satisfying the recursion condition. Let <math>h_{\beta} : \beta \to X</math> be given by <math>\gamma \mapsto G(g_{\beta}|_{\gamma})</math>. In the limit case; i.e., <math>\alpha</math> is a limit ordinal, identifying functions with their graphs, consider the union
:<math>\bigcup_{\beta < \alpha} h_{\beta}.</math>
The formation of a union is justified by the axiom of union but for the above union to be a set, we need the collection
:<math>\{ h_{\beta} \mid \beta < \alpha \}</math>
to be a set; in other words, the image of the map <math>\beta \mapsto h_{\beta}</math> to be a set and that is ensured by the axiom of replacement. Finally, this union is the graph of a function <math>f : \alpha \to X</math> that satisfies the required recursion condition. The successor case is handled similarly. <math>\square</math>
